source.title: Understanding Inhibition Through Maximally Tense Images
source.authors: Christopher J. Hamblin; Srijani Saha; Talia Konkle; George A. Alvarez

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly replicates toy-model experiments on sparse features and bottlenecks, but evaluates interference through attribution matrices rather than directly measuring the original claim’s feature-direction geometry. It also tests an XOR toy task and measures shared attribution images in InceptionV1.
record.gate_note: Rows record the toy-model attribution results relevant to superposition and the InceptionV1 uniqueness results. The reported importance weights for toy features are a training choice, not a separate result about how importance changes geometry. The paper's attribution-completeness, visualization, and human-experiment results do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper replicates the toy absolute-value model at hidden widths m = 12, 10, 8 and 6, adds an XOR variant, and measures interference. It does this through layer-to-feature attribution matrices rather than weight geometry, so it is a different method aimed at the same question. The InceptionV1 uniqueness result is about a vision model, not an LLM, so it does not bear on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that superposition is a major obstacle to analysing inhibition: networks use negative weights as part of a compression scheme that represents more features than units, and interference produces the same +/- attribution motif as functionally relevant tension. Deeper InceptionV1 layers show high attribution to the same images across many features, as superposition predicts. They say clean analysis will likely need monosemantic disentanglement methods like those used for LLMs.
record.recipe_differences: The paper describes its absolute-value toy-model experiment as a replication and uses a similar sparse-input, hidden-width comparison, but analyzes layer-to-feature attributions rather than directly establishing feature-direction geometry. It also adds an XOR task.
record.method_sensitivity: The amount of off-diagonal attribution changes with hidden width. For InceptionV1, image-selection uniqueness changes with depth and with L1 versus L2 attribution-norm selection.

fits_no_version.finding: In deeper InceptionV1 layers, many unit and k-means features share the same top-attribution images. Uniqueness is near ceiling for MEIs but drops for attribution-selected images, and L2 selection mitigates the drop somewhat compared with L1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision CNNs show signs consistent with superposition in deeper layers: the same inputs drive large attributions across many features.

record.problems: The toy-model evidence is qualitative attribution evidence, not a direct measurement of feature-direction angles or regular geometry. The toy experiments use a fixed sparsity setting, so they do not establish a sparsity-dependent transition. The InceptionV1 uniqueness results are shown as plots without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise eligible claim-related results were omitted.

untested.parts: No sweep of feature sparsity, so no sparsity-dependent transition. Sparsity is fixed at 0.99 for abs and 0.95 for XOR. No direct measurement of near-orthogonality or of regular geometric arrangements of feature directions.
Importance weights (0.9^i) are used in training, but the study never reports which features get dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No LLM or SAE experiments; the real-model test is on InceptionV1 (vision).

missing.what: Toy-model loss rises as hidden width shrinks and increases monotonically with the number of simultaneously active features. This matches superposition theory: features are represented faithfully alone but not together. The m = 12 models have zero loss.

Images among the top-100 attributions for at least 15 of 20 sampled features each show a single salient concept (e.g. 'dog-face', 'bird'). The authors read this as superposed features rather than images containing many features.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. All toy evidence is qualitative (Figure 7 matrices, no numbers). The toy models were chosen as the best of 1000 seeds. The main contribution is MTI visualization, and most of the paper does not bear on the claim.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments vary hidden width but do not sweep feature sparsity or directly measure near-orthogonality or regular geometric arrangements of feature directions.
Although absolute-value toy features are assigned unequal importance weights, the study does not report whether importance determines dedicated dimensions or sharing.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The real-model experiment is on InceptionV1, not an LLM; it does not test LLM feature spread or SAE recovery.
The study does not evaluate SAE features as complete, stable, or canonical model units.
The study does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: absolute value model
rows.size_stated: input x ∈ R6; hidden dimensions m = 12
rows.operation_detail: Computed layer-to-output-feature positive and negative attribution for basis-vector inputs and their negatives.

conditions.value: ei and −ei for each of six input features

rows.measure: Off-diagonal attribution between input features and output features in the hidden layer
rows.value: Attribution was positive on the diagonal only and zero elsewhere; the authors describe this model as disentangled.
rows.note: Reference condition without reported off-diagonal interference; this is not a setting with more features than hidden dimensions.
rows.check: Control row. The m = 12 model can compute abs exactly, so the absence of off-diagonal attribution is the expected no-bottleneck baseline. It is not evidence against V1.

rows.subject: XOR toy model
rows.size_stated: input in R12; hidden dimensions m = 12
rows.operation_detail: Computed layer-to-output-feature positive and negative attribution for inputs [1, 0]i and [1, 1]i.

conditions.value: XOR over six independent pairs of input features

rows.measure: Positive and negative attribution from the paired input features to the XOR output feature
rows.value: For [1, 1]i, the disentangled model shows simultaneous excitation and inhibition of the relevant output feature; the paper attributes these to separate latent ‘or’ and ‘and’ features.
rows.note: This is functionally relevant inhibition, not evidence by itself of superposition; the measure does not establish the claimed direction geometry.
rows.check: The disentangled XOR model's simultaneous excitation and inhibition is functional ('or' vs 'and' latent features), not superposition interference. It should be the baseline for r6–r8, not a row linked to V1.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared uniqueness of selected high-attribution images across sampled unit features and layers using the L1 attribution norm.

conditions.value: unit features; 20 random units per layer
MTIs selected by L1 attribution norm

rows.measure: Uniqueness of selected images across features
rows.baseline: MEI image uniqueness across layers is described as near ceiling
rows.value: Uniqueness decreases substantially in deeper layers compared with MEIs.
rows.note: The text describes the trend, but the plotted values are not stated numerically. This is a vision-model result, not an LLM test.
rows.check: Vision-model result framed by the authors as consistent with superposition. It is not an LLM test, so it does not bear on V4.

relationships.condition: Sparse-input toy ReLU models (abs and XOR, 6 features) with hidden width m = 10, 8, 6 versus disentangled m = 12
relationships.reason: Off-diagonal attribution is zero at m = 12 (r1) and grows as the bottleneck tightens (r2–r4, r6–r8). This is qualitative, figure-based evidence of interference, not of geometry.
relationships.display_finding: Off-diagonal attribution was zero at m = 12 and grew as the hidden width tightened to 10, 8 and 6. This shows interference qualitatively, not geometry.

relation.reason: Its own bottleneck experiments test whether independent features produce interfering representations and off-diagonal attribution.

tranche.reason: Replicates sparse toy computations but measures interference through positive and negative attribution matrices rather than representation geometry.

source_check.notes: Attribution results are qualitative; XOR bottlenecks are described collectively rather than separately by width. Appendix G checks task performance; Appendix F reports ranges for inversion validation, not uncertainty on the toy interference results.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Absolute-value and XOR toy models with bottleneck hidden dimensions m = 10, 8, and 6
reader_labels.reason: Off-diagonal attribution appears in bottleneck models and increases as the absolute-value model narrows; bottleneck XOR models also show large off-diagonal attribution (r2–r4, r6–r8). This supports interference in the tested toy settings, but does not establish the claimed regular direction geometry.
